name: Science trivia (hard)
description: 50 hard questions about physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, the human body, inventions. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: A white dwarf is held up against its own gravity by which quantum effect, whose failure at high enough mass defines the Chandrasekhar limit?
items.explain: Above the limit, electron degeneracy pressure in the star's core can no longer balance gravitational self-attraction, so the white dwarf cannot remain stable.

items.question: Roughly what is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf star, known as the Chandrasekhar limit?
items.explain: Chandrasekhar's calculation gave a limit of about 1.44 solar masses, above which the star continues to collapse.

items.question: Which astrophysicist calculated the maximum mass of a white dwarf while sailing from India to England to begin graduate study at Cambridge?
items.explain: Chandrasekhar worked out the limit, about 1.44 times the mass of the Sun, on the 1930 voyage from India to Cambridge.

items.question: Which type of supernova is thought to occur when a white dwarf accretes enough matter to tip over the Chandrasekhar limit?
items.explain: Type Ia supernovae are thought to result when a white dwarf gains enough mass to pass the Chandrasekhar limit and collapses catastrophically.

items.question: In water, light slows to roughly what fraction of its vacuum speed, allowing fast charged particles to outrun it and produce Cherenkov radiation?
items.explain: Light travels at about 75 percent of its vacuum speed in water, so energetic particles from nuclear fuel can exceed it and give off a blue glow.

items.question: Pavel Cherenkov shared the 1958 Nobel Prize in Physics with Ilya Frank and which other physicist?
items.explain: The 1958 physics prize went to Cherenkov, Frank and Tamm for experimentally demonstrating and explaining the Cherenkov glow.

items.question: A charged particle in a transparent medium of refractive index n emits Cherenkov radiation only if its speed exceeds what?
answers: The vacuum light speed times n
The speed of sound in the medium
The vacuum light speed divided by n
items.correct: The vacuum light speed divided by n
items.explain: Light travels at c/n in the medium. Particles slower than c/n produce no Cherenkov radiation.

items.question: In the chain of middle-ear ossicles, which bone sits between the malleus (hammer) and the stapes (stirrup)?
items.explain: The incus (anvil) bridges the malleus and stapes, passing sound vibrations from the eardrum toward the cochlea.

items.question: The footplate of the stapes transmits sound vibrations into the inner ear through which opening of the cochlea?
items.explain: The stapes footplate sits in the oval window and passes vibrations into the fluid-filled cochlea.

items.question: What does the stapedius muscle, widely cited as the smallest skeletal muscle, do in response to a loud noise?
answers: Relaxes so the stapes vibrates more freely
Shifts the incus away from the malleus
Pumps fluid out of the cochlea
items.explain: The stapedius contracts and pulls on the annular ligament, which stops the stapes from moving too much.

source.title: Uncovering the Mighty Role of the Tiniest - A Guide to the Smallest Bone in the Human Body! - Healthwire

items.question: At which German university did Fritz Haber develop his 1909 laboratory method for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen?
items.explain: Haber worked at the University of Karlsruhe when he demonstrated high-pressure ammonia synthesis in 1909.

items.question: The first industrial ammonia plant using the Haber-Bosch process began operating in 1913 at which German site?
items.explain: Carl Bosch's team at BASF scaled up Haber's method, and the first industrial plant started up at Oppau in 1913.

items.question: Which metal served as the catalyst in Fritz Haber's original 1909 laboratory synthesis of ammonia?
items.explain: Haber reacted nitrogen with hydrogen under high temperature and pressure using an osmium catalyst. Iron-based catalysts came with industrialisation.

items.question: Who received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the synthesis of ammonia from its elements?
items.explain: Haber won the 1918 chemistry prize. Carl Bosch shared a later prize, in 1931, for high-pressure chemical engineering.

items.question: To build a commercial ammonia plant, Carl Bosch and colleagues tested roughly how many catalysts?
items.explain: Bosch and his coworkers tested over 2,500 catalysts and developed the high-pressure, high-temperature equipment the process needed.

items.question: Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, is made by reacting which two chemicals?
items.explain: Leo Baekeland controlled the phenol-formaldehyde condensation reaction under heat and pressure to produce Bakelite.

items.question: Bakelite replaced hard rubber and which natural resin in the early electric power industry and home appliances?
items.explain: Because of its excellent insulating properties, Bakelite replaced shellac and hard rubber in electrical uses.

items.question: Which early cellulose-based plastic, invented decades before Bakelite, was one of the world's first plastics?
items.explain: Celluloid was made from modified natural cellulose. Bakelite came more than 40 years later as the first wholly synthetic plastic.

source.title: Leo Hendrick Baekeland and the Invention of Bakelite®

items.question: What name did Leo Baekeland give to the heated pressure vessels in which he formed Bakelite?
items.explain: Baekeland called his machines "Bakelizers". The original was used from 1907 to 1910 to react phenol and formaldehyde under pressure.

source.title: Leo Hendrick Baekeland and the Invention of Bakelite®

items.question: According to Oregon State volcanologists, the absence of what process on Mars let its giant shield volcanoes just keep growing?
items.explain: Without moving plates, Martian volcanoes could keep growing in one place, limited only by the volume of lava available.

items.question: Before space probes revealed it to be a volcano, astronomers knew Olympus Mons as a bright albedo feature with what Latin name?
items.explain: Nix Olympica ("Olympic Snow") was observed from Earth in the late 19th century. Mariner 9 showed in 1971 that it was an immense volcano.

items.question: Roughly what is the average slope of Olympus Mons, which gives the shield volcano its low, squat profile?
items.explain: Shield volcanoes form as lava flows slowly down their sides, so Olympus Mons has an average slope of only about 5 percent.

source.title: Olympus Mons: The largest volcano in the solar system

items.question: What is the name of the dried-out, curled-up form a tardigrade takes during cryptobiosis?
items.explain: A tardigrade expels most of its body water, retracts its head and legs, and curls into a dried ball called a tun.

source.title: What are tardigrades and why are they nearly indestructible?

items.question: Which German scientist first identified the tardigrade's suspended state in 1922, calling it a tönnchenform, later shortened to "tun"?
items.explain: H. Baumann coined tönnchenform in 1922 for the barrel-shaped dormant state, and the term was later shortened to tun.

items.question: In the tun state, a tardigrade's metabolism drops to roughly what fraction of normal levels?
items.explain: Entering the tun slows the tardigrade's metabolism drastically, to near 0.01 percent of normal levels.

items.question: Which Krebs cycle enzyme is anchored in the inner mitochondrial membrane instead of lying in the matrix with the others?
items.explain: Most Krebs cycle enzymes are in the mitochondrial matrix. Succinate dehydrogenase is the exception, locked into the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.question: In which year did Hans Adolf Krebs first propose the cycle that now bears his name?
items.explain: Krebs first proposed the citric acid cycle in 1937.

items.question: The regeneration of which compound completes each turn of the Krebs cycle?
items.explain: Acetyl-CoA is the starting point of the cycle. Oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end, which closes the loop.

source.title: Krebs Cycle or Citric Acid Cycle

items.question: A day on Titan lasts as long as the time it takes Titan to orbit Saturn. About how long is that?
items.explain: A Titan day lasts about 15 days and 22 hours, equal to its orbital period around Saturn.

items.question: Cassini radar scans showed that which large Titan sea is mostly pure liquid methane, rather than the ethane scientists expected?
items.explain: Scientists expected Ligeia Mare to be mostly ethane, but Cassini radar data showed it is predominantly liquid methane.

source.title: ESA - Profile of a methane sea on Titan

items.question: Radio signals measured during the Huygens probe's descent strongly suggested an ocean at what depth beneath Titan's surface?
items.explain: Huygens measured radio signals during its descent that strongly suggested an ocean 35 to 50 miles (55 to 80 km) below the surface.

items.question: Walther Meissner discovered the expulsion of magnetic fields from superconductors in 1933 with which colleague?
items.explain: The effect is named for Meissner and Ochsenfeld, the German physicists who discovered it in 1933.

items.question: Meissner and Ochsenfeld discovered the effect by measuring the magnetic flux outside specimens of which two metals as they were cooled?
items.explain: In 1933 they measured the flux distribution outside tin and lead specimens cooled below their transition temperature in a magnetic field.

items.question: A superconductor in the Meissner state is a perfect diamagnet. What magnetic susceptibility does it have?
items.explain: Surface currents create a magnetization equal and opposite to the applied field, giving a magnetic susceptibility of -1.

items.question: In which year did Dmitri Mendeleev predict the existence of gallium, along with its low melting point and density?
items.explain: Mendeleev predicted gallium in 1871, before it was discovered, and accurately forecast key properties such as its density and low melting point.

items.question: The melting point of gallium, about 29.76 °C, is a formal fixed reference point on which temperature scale?
items.explain: Gallium's melting point is one of the formal temperature reference points of ITS-90, set by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures.

items.question: Which common metal's structure does liquid gallium infiltrate and weaken, so that a drink can can be pierced with a thumb?
items.explain: Liquid gallium infiltrates aluminium's structure and compromises its integrity, making a can feel like tin foil.

items.question: Which PhD student of Rosalind Franklin worked with her at King's College London to take the famous X-ray image known as Photograph 51?
items.explain: Franklin took Photograph 51 together with her PhD student Raymond Gosling at King's College London in May 1952.

items.question: According to Franklin's lab notebook, DNA was exposed to X-rays for how long to take Photograph 51?
items.explain: Franklin's notebook records a total of 62 hours of X-ray exposure for Photograph 51.

items.question: In which journal was Photograph 51 published on 25 April 1953, alongside Watson and Crick's double-helix model?
items.explain: Franklin and Gosling's paper appeared in Nature on 25 April 1953, next to the Watson and Crick paper presenting the double helix.

items.question: Photo 51 captured which highly hydrated form of DNA, rather than the drier A form that doesn't show a distinct helical structure?
items.explain: Photo 51 shows the hydrated B form of DNA, whose diffraction pattern revealed the helical structure much more clearly.

items.question: Which mathematician worked out the first three collinear Lagrange points in 1765, seven years before Lagrange's own publication?
items.explain: Euler solved the gravitational equations in 1765 and found L1, L2 and L3, which lie on a straight line.

source.title: James Webb telescope is headed for Lagrange point 2

items.question: The James Webb Space Telescope is not parked at L2 but orbits it. How long does one circuit of its halo orbit take?
items.explain: Webb orbits L2 in a large halo orbit that takes about 168 days to complete one circuit.

source.title: Webb's Orbit at Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2 (L2)

items.question: Roughly how many times farther from Earth than the Moon is the Sun-Earth L2 point?
items.explain: L2 lies about 1.5 million km from Earth, roughly four times the Earth-Moon distance.

source.title: Webb's Orbit at Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2 (L2)

items.question: Which two Lagrange points sit at the tips of equilateral triangles formed with the two large bodies?
items.explain: L1, L2 and L3 lie in a line with the two large bodies, while L4 and L5 sit at the points of equilateral triangles.

items.question: Which mineral is the reference for hardness 5 on the Mohs scale?
items.explain: The scale runs talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz, topaz, corundum, diamond. That puts apatite at 5.

source.title: Mohs Hardness Scale: Testing the Resistance to Being Scratched

items.question: On the Mohs scale's absolute hardness, diamond (10) is about how many times as hard as corundum (9)?
items.explain: The Mohs scale is ordinal, not linear. Diamond is roughly four times as hard as corundum in absolute terms.

items.question: In which year did German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs create his scale of mineral hardness?
items.explain: Mohs created the scale in 1812, using ten readily available minerals from talc to diamond.

source.title: Mohs scale of mineral hardness - New World Encyclopedia

items.question: Which physicist applied the Pauli exclusion principle in developing quantum electrodynamics, leading him to predict the positron?
items.explain: Dirac pioneered quantum electrodynamics and applied the exclusion principle to predict the existence of the positron.

items.question: In 1940 Wolfgang Pauli proved a necessary connection between which two properties of a particle?
items.explain: Pauli showed that particles with half-integer spin must be fermions and obey the exclusion principle, while integer-spin particles must be bosons.
